question: Why do we use standard precautions in the hospital ward?

options.A: To lower the cost of purchasing expensive surgical gloves
options.B: To reduce the risk of transmitting infections from body fluids
options.C: To treat patients who have diagnosed infectious diseases
options.D: To completely eliminate bacteria from the hospital ward

explanation: You've got this! Standard precautions are our everyday shield to stop germs in blood and body fluids from spreading to us or other patients.

question: Which body fluid is usually NOT covered under standard precautions?
explanation: Great try! Sweat doesn't carry bloodborne infections, so unless there is visible blood in it, standard precautions don't apply to it.

question: When must a nurse choose soap and water instead of an alcohol hand rub?

options.A: Before touching a patient who has intact skin
options.B: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids
options.C: When entering a clean general medical ward
options.D: After taking a patient's temperature with a digital thermometer

explanation: Spot on! Alcohol rubs are great, but they can't wash away physical dirt. When your hands look or feel dirty, good old soap and water is a must.

question: How long should you rub your hands together with an alcohol-based sanitizer?
explanation: You got it! Giving it 20 to 30 seconds ensures the sanitizer covers every part of your hands and kills the germs effectively.

question: Why do you still need to wash your hands right after taking off disposable gloves?

options.A: Sweat trapped inside the gloves creates a barrier that requires washing
options.B: Hospital policy requires hand washing only when gloves are completely absent
options.C: Soap activates the residual chemical powder left inside the glove material
options.D: Gloves can have tiny invisible holes or tears that allow germs through

explanation: Exactly! Gloves aren't foolproof, and microscopic tears happen. Plus, your hands can easily pick up germs while taking the gloves off. Always sanitize after!

question: You are assisting with a wound wash and fluid is likely to splash. What PPE do you need?

options.A: Gloves and a standard cloth surgical cap only
options.B: Gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection
options.C: Sterile surgical gloves and a paper face mask only
options.D: A heavy rubber apron and heavy-duty utility boots

explanation: Well done! Whenever there's a risk of splashing, you want full protection—hands, body, face, and eyes—to keep yourself safe.

question: What is the safest thing to do with a used needle and syringe right after an injection?

options.A: Drop it directly into a rigid safety box without recapping
options.B: Recap the needle carefully using both hands to protect others
options.C: Place the syringe on the medication tray for later disposal
options.D: Break the needle off the syringe barrel using your fingers

explanation: Spot on! Never recap needles. Dropping them straight into the safety box is the #1 way to prevent accidental pricks.

question: When should a sharps safety box be sealed and replaced?

options.A: At the end of every single shift
options.B: When it is about three-quarters full
options.C: Once a week regardless of its contents
options.D: When it is completely overflowing to the top

explanation: You've got it! Sealing it at three-quarters full stops needles from poking out the top and injuring someone.

question: Where should you cough or sneeze if you don't have a tissue nearby?

options.A: Into your inner elbow or upper sleeve
options.B: Directly onto your clean uniform sleeve
options.C: Directly into the palm of your bare hand
options.D: Into the air away from other people

explanation: Brilliant! Coughing into your elbow keeps germs off your hands, preventing you from transferring them to door handles and patients.

question: What is the main point of cough etiquette in a busy clinic waiting area?

options.A: To contain respiratory droplets at the source and stop germ spread
options.B: To prevent the buildup of dust particles on furniture
options.C: To cure patients who suffer from chronic lung diseases
options.D: To eliminate the need for healthcare workers to wear face masks

explanation: Exactly! Catching those droplets early stops airborne bugs from floating around and infecting everyone in the waiting room.

question: Which surfaces in a patient's room need cleaning and disinfecting the most often?

options.A: The outer walls of the hospital storage cupboard
options.B: High ceilings and ceiling fan blades
options.C: High-touch surfaces like bed rails and door handles
options.D: The lower baseboards near the floor corners

explanation: You're right! Bed rails and door handles are touched constantly by hands, so they collect germs the fastest.

question: When cleaning a hospital room, what general direction should you follow?

options.A: From the cleanest areas to the dirtiest areas
options.B: From the floor upwards to the furniture tops
options.C: From the corners towards the middle of the ceiling
options.D: Randomly based on where the most visible dust is

explanation: Well done! Moving from clean to dirty ensures you don't drag heavy dirt and germs onto surfaces you just wiped clean.

question: What is the very first thing you should do after a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water
options.B: Squeeze the puncture site firmly to force the blood out
options.C: Cover the bleeding wound tightly with an adhesive bandage
options.D: Apply a strong antiseptic bleach solution directly inside

explanation: Don't panic—your first step is always to wash the area well with soap and running water to rinse away surface contaminants.

question: Why must you report a needle-stick injury to your supervisor immediately?

options.A: To ensure the nurse receives disciplinary punishment for carelessness
options.B: To complete administrative paperwork for the hospital insurance policy
options.C: To replace the broken needle with a brand new syringe
options.D: To allow prompt medical evaluation and timely post-exposure prophylaxis

explanation: Spot on! Time matters with needle pricks. Getting quick medical advice and early preventive medication (PEP) keeps you safe.
